stem: The following concentrations were obtained for the formation of \(\text{NH}_3\) from \(\text{N}_2\) and \(\text{H}_2\) at equilibrium at 500 K. \([\text{N}_2] = 1.5 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{M}\), \([\text{H}_2] = 3.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{M}\) and \([\text{NH}_3] = 1.2 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{M}\). Calculate equilibrium constant.
solution:
The equilibrium constant for the reaction, \(\text{N}_2(g) + 3\text{H}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NH}_3(g)\) can be written as,

\(K_c = \dfrac{[\text{NH}_3(g)]^2}{[\text{N}_2(g)][\text{H}_2(g)]^3}\)

\(= \dfrac{(1.2 \times 10^{-2})^2}{(1.5 \times 10^{-2})(3.0 \times 10^{-2})^3}\)

\(= 0.355 \times 10^3 = 3.55 \times 10^2\)

subtopic: Law of Chemical Equilibrium and Equilibrium Constant
stem:
At equilibrium, the concentrations of \(\text{N}_2 = 3.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{M}\), \(\text{O}_2 = 4.2 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{M}\) and \(\text{NO} = 2.8 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{M}\) in a sealed vessel at 800 K. What will be \(K_c\) for the reaction

\(\text{N}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}(g)\)
solution:
For the reaction equilibrium constant, \(K_c\) can be written as,

\(K_c = \dfrac{[\text{NO}]^2}{[\text{N}_2][\text{O}_2]}\)

\(= \dfrac{(2.8 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{M})^2}{(3.0 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{M})(4.2 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{M})}\)

\(= 0.622\)

stem:
\(\text{PCl}_5\), \(\text{PCl}_3\) and \(\text{Cl}_2\) are at equilibrium at 500 K and having concentration \(1.59\,\text{M}\) \(\text{PCl}_3\), \(1.59\,\text{M}\) \(\text{Cl}_2\) and \(1.41\,\text{M}\) \(\text{PCl}_5\). Calculate \(K_c\) for the reaction,

\(\text{PCl}_5 \rightleftharpoons \text{PCl}_3 + \text{Cl}_2\)
solution:
The equilibrium constant \(K_c\) for the above reaction can be written as,

\(K_c = \dfrac{[\text{PCl}_3][\text{Cl}_2]}{[\text{PCl}_5]} = \dfrac{(1.59)^2}{(1.41)} = 1.79\)

stem:
The value of \(K_c = 4.24\) at 800 K for the reaction,

\(\text{CO}(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2(g)\)

Calculate equilibrium concentrations of \(\text{CO}_2\), \(\text{H}_2\), \(\text{CO}\) and \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) at 800 K, if only \(\text{CO}\) and \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) are present initially at concentrations of \(0.10\,\text{M}\) each.
solution:
For the reaction,

\(\text{CO}(g) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(g) \rightleftharpoons \text{CO}_2(g) + \text{H}_2(g)\)

Initial concentration: \(0.1\,\text{M}\), \(0.1\,\text{M}\), 0, 0.

Let \(x\) mole per litre of each of the product be formed.

At equilibrium: \((0.1-x)\,\text{M}\), \((0.1-x)\,\text{M}\), \(x\,\text{M}\), \(x\,\text{M}\), where \(x\) is the amount of \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{H}_2\) at equilibrium.

Hence, equilibrium constant can be written as,

\(K_c = x^2/(0.1-x)^2 = 4.24\)

\(x^2 = 4.24(0.01 + x^2 - 0.2x)\)

\(x^2 = 0.0424 + 4.24x^2 - 0.848x\)

\(3.24x^2 - 0.848x + 0.0424 = 0\)

\(a = 3.24\), \(b = -0.848\), \(c = 0.0424\)

(for quadratic equation \(ax^2 + bx + c = 0\), \(x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\))

\(x = [0.848 \pm \sqrt{(0.848)^2 - 4(3.24)(0.0424)}]/(3.24 \times 2)\)

\(x = (0.848 \pm 0.4118)/6.48\)

\(x_1 = (0.848 - 0.4118)/6.48 = 0.067\)

\(x_2 = (0.848 + 0.4118)/6.48 = 0.194\)

The value 0.194 should be neglected because it will give concentration of the reactant which is more than initial concentration.

Hence the equilibrium concentrations are,

\([\text{CO}_2] = [\text{H}_2] = x = 0.067\,\text{M}\)

\([\text{CO}] = [\text{H}_2\text{O}] = 0.1 - 0.067 = 0.033\,\text{M}\)

stem:
For the equilibrium,

\(2\text{NOCl}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g)\)

the value of the equilibrium constant, \(K_c\) is \(3.75 \times 10^{-6}\) at 1069 K. Calculate the \(K_p\) for the reaction at this temperature?
solution:
We know that,

\(K_p = K_c(\text{R}T)^{\Delta n}\)

For the above reaction,

\(\Delta n = (2+1) - 2 = 1\)

\(K_p = 3.75 \times 10^{-6}(0.0831 \times 1069)\)

\(K_p = 0.033\)

stem:
The value of \(K_p\) for the reaction,

\(\text{CO}_2(g) + \text{C}(s) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{CO}(g)\)

is 3.0 at 1000 K. If initially \(p_{\text{CO}_2} = 0.48\,\text{bar}\) and \(p_{\text{CO}} = 0\,\text{bar}\) and pure graphite is present, calculate the equilibrium partial pressures of \(\text{CO}\) and \(\text{CO}_2\).
solution:
For the reaction, let \(x\) be the decrease in pressure of \(\text{CO}_2\), then

\(\text{CO}_2(g) + \text{C}(s) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{CO}(g)\)

Initial pressure: \(0.48\,\text{bar}\), \(0\)

At equilibrium: \((0.48 - x)\,\text{bar}\), \(2x\,\text{bar}\)

\(K_p = \dfrac{p_{\text{CO}}^2}{p_{\text{CO}_2}}\)

\(K_p = (2x)^2/(0.48 - x) = 3\)

\(4x^2 = 3(0.48 - x)\)

\(4x^2 = 1.44 - x\)

\(4x^2 + 3x - 1.44 = 0\)

\(a = 4\), \(b = 3\), \(c = -1.44\)

\(x = \dfrac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a}\)

\(= [-3 \pm \sqrt{(3)^2 - 4(4)(-1.44)}]/(2 \times 4)\)

\(= (-3 \pm 5.66)/8\)

\(= (-3 + 5.66)/8\) (as value of \(x\) cannot be negative hence we neglect that value)

\(x = 2.66/8 = 0.33\)

The equilibrium partial pressures are,

\(p_{\text{CO}} = 2x = 2 \times 0.33 = 0.66\,\text{bar}\)

\(p_{\text{CO}_2} = 0.48 - x = 0.48 - 0.33 = 0.15\,\text{bar}\)
_note: Book defect preserved in intent: the printed solution labels BOTH final partial pressures as p_CO2 — the first (2x = 0.66 bar) is the pressure of CO, as its own working (K_p = p_CO^2/p_CO2) requires. The label has been set to p_CO here because printing it as p_CO2 would make the solution self-contradictory.

stem: The value of \(K_c\) for the reaction \(2\text{A} \rightleftharpoons \text{B} + \text{C}\) is \(2 \times 10^{-3}\). At a given time, the composition of reaction mixture is \([\text{A}] = [\text{B}] = [\text{C}] = 3 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{M}\). In which direction the reaction will proceed?
solution:
For the reaction the reaction quotient \(Q_c\) is given by,

\(Q_c = [\text{B}][\text{C}]/[\text{A}]^2\)

as \([\text{A}] = [\text{B}] = [\text{C}] = 3 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{M}\)

\(Q_c = (3 \times 10^{-4})(3 \times 10^{-4})/(3 \times 10^{-4})^2 = 1\)

as \(Q_c > K_c\) so the reaction will proceed in the reverse direction.

stem:
\(13.8\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{N}_2\text{O}_4\) was placed in a \(1\,\text{L}\) reaction vessel at 400 K and allowed to attain equilibrium

\(\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}_2(g)\)

The total pressure at equilibrium was found to be \(9.15\,\text{bar}\). Calculate \(K_c\), \(K_p\) and partial pressure at equilibrium.
solution:
We know \(pV = n\text{R}T\)

Total volume \((V) = 1\,\text{L}\)

Molecular mass of \(\text{N}_2\text{O}_4 = 92\,\text{g}\)

Number of moles \(= 13.8\,\text{g}/92\,\text{g} = 0.15\) of the gas \((n)\)

Gas constant \((\text{R}) = 0.083\,\text{bar L mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}\)

Temperature \((T) = 400\,\text{K}\)

\(p \times 1\,\text{L} = 0.15\,\text{mol} \times 0.083\,\text{bar L mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1} \times 400\,\text{K}\)

\(p = 4.98\,\text{bar}\)

\(\text{N}_2\text{O}_4 \rightleftharpoons 2\text{NO}_2\)

Initial pressure: \(4.98\,\text{bar}\), \(0\)

At equilibrium: \((4.98 - x)\,\text{bar}\), \(2x\,\text{bar}\)

Hence, \(p_{\text{total}}\) at equilibrium \(= p_{\text{N}_2\text{O}_4} + p_{\text{NO}_2}\)

\(9.15 = (4.98 - x) + 2x\)

\(9.15 = 4.98 + x\)

\(x = 9.15 - 4.98 = 4.17\,\text{bar}\)

Partial pressures at equilibrium are,

\(p_{\text{N}_2\text{O}_4} = 4.98 - 4.17 = 0.81\,\text{bar}\)

\(p_{\text{NO}_2} = 2x = 2 \times 4.17 = 8.34\,\text{bar}\)

\(K_p = (p_{\text{NO}_2})^2/p_{\text{N}_2\text{O}_4} = (8.34)^2/0.81 = 85.87\)

\(K_p = K_c(\text{R}T)^{\Delta n}\)

\(85.87 = K_c(0.083 \times 400)^1\)

\(K_c = 2.586 = 2.6\)

stem: The value of \(\Delta G^\ominus\) for the phosphorylation of glucose in glycolysis is \(13.8\,\text{kJ/mol}\). Find the value of \(K_c\) at 298 K.
solution:
\(\Delta G^\ominus = 13.8\,\text{kJ/mol} = 13.8 \times 10^3\,\text{J/mol}\)

Also, \(\Delta G^\ominus = -\text{R}T \ln K_c\)

Hence, \(\ln K_c = \dfrac{-13.8 \times 10^3\,\text{J/mol}}{8.314\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1} \times 298\,\text{K}}\)

\(\ln K_c = -5.569\)

\(K_c = e^{-5.569}\)

\(K_c = 3.81 \times 10^{-3}\)

Hydrolysis of sucrose gives,

Sucrose \(+\ \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons\) Glucose \(+\) Fructose

Equilibrium constant \(K_c\) for the reaction is \(2 \times 10^{13}\) at 300 K. Calculate \(\Delta G^\ominus\) at 300 K.
solution:
\(\Delta G^\ominus = -\text{R}T \ln K_c\)

\(\Delta G^\ominus = -8.314\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1} \times 300\,\text{K} \times \ln(2 \times 10^{13})\)

\(\Delta G^\ominus = -7.64 \times 10^4\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\)

stem: What will be the conjugate bases for the following Brönsted acids: \(\text{HF}\), \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\) and \(\text{HCO}_3^-\)?
solution: The conjugate bases should have one proton less in each case and therefore the corresponding conjugate bases are: \(\text{F}^-\), \(\text{HSO}_4^-\) and \(\text{CO}_3^{2-}\) respectively.

stem: Write the conjugate acids for the following Brönsted bases: \(\text{NH}_2^-\), \(\text{NH}_3\) and \(\text{HCOO}^-\).
solution: The conjugate acid should have one extra proton in each case and therefore the corresponding conjugate acids are: \(\text{NH}_3\), \(\text{NH}_4^+\) and \(\text{HCOOH}\) respectively.

solution:

stem:
Classify the following species into Lewis acids and Lewis bases and show how these act as such:

(a) \(\text{HO}^-\)  (b) \(\text{F}^-\)  (c) \(\text{H}^+\)  (d) \(\text{BCl}_3\)
solution:
(a) Hydroxyl ion is a Lewis base as it can donate an electron lone pair \((:\text{OH}^-)\).

(b) Flouride ion acts as a Lewis base as it can donate any one of its four electron lone pairs.

(c) A proton is a Lewis acid as it can accept a lone pair of electrons from bases like hydroxyl ion and fluoride ion.

(d) \(\text{BCl}_3\) acts as a Lewis acid as it can accept a lone pair of electrons from species like ammonia or amine molecules.

stem: The concentration of hydrogen ion in a sample of soft drink is \(3.8 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{M}\). What is its pH?
solution:
\(\text{pH} = -\log[3.8 \times 10^{-3}]\)

\(= -\{\log[3.8] + \log[10^{-3}]\}\)

\(= -\{(0.58) + (-3.0)\} = -\{-2.42\} = 2.42\)

Therefore, the pH of the soft drink is 2.42 and it can be inferred that it is acidic.

stem: Calculate pH of a \(1.0 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{M}\) solution of \(\text{HCl}\).
solution:
\(2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq) + \text{OH}^-(aq)\)

\(K_w = [\text{OH}^-][\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = 10^{-14}\)

Let, \(x = [\text{OH}^-] = [\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]\) from \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\). The \(\text{H}_3\text{O}^+\) concentration is generated (i) from the ionization of \(\text{HCl}\) dissolved i.e.,

\(\text{HCl}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq) + \text{Cl}^-(aq)\),

and (ii) from ionization of \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\). In these very dilute solutions, both sources of \(\text{H}_3\text{O}^+\) must be considered:

\([\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = 10^{-8} + x\)

\(K_w = (10^{-8} + x)(x) = 10^{-14}\)

or \(x^2 + 10^{-8}x - 10^{-14} = 0\)

\([\text{OH}^-] = x = 9.5 \times 10^{-8}\)

So, \(\text{pOH} = 7.02\) and \(\text{pH} = 6.98\)

stem: The ionization constant of \(\text{HF}\) is \(3.2 \times 10^{-4}\). Calculate the degree of dissociation of \(\text{HF}\) in its \(0.02\,\text{M}\) solution. Calculate the concentration of all species present (\(\text{H}_3\text{O}^+\), \(\text{F}^-\) and \(\text{HF}\)) in the solution and its pH.
solution:
The following proton transfer reactions are possible:

1) \(\text{HF} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_3\text{O}^+ + \text{F}^-\)   \(K_a = 3.2 \times 10^{-4}\)

2) \(\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_3\text{O}^+ + \text{OH}^-\)   \(K_w = 1.0 \times 10^{-14}\)

As \(K_a \gg K_w\), [1] is the principle reaction.

\(\text{HF} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_3\text{O}^+ + \text{F}^-\)

Initial concentration (M): \(0.02\), \(0\), \(0\)

Change (M): \(-0.02\alpha\), \(+0.02\alpha\), \(+0.02\alpha\)

Equilibrium concentration (M): \(0.02 - 0.02\alpha\), \(0.02\alpha\), \(0.02\alpha\)

Substituting equilibrium concentrations in the equilibrium reaction for principal reaction gives:

\(K_a = (0.02\alpha)^2/(0.02 - 0.02\alpha) = 0.02\alpha^2/(1-\alpha) = 3.2 \times 10^{-4}\)

We obtain the following quadratic equation:

\(\alpha^2 + 1.6 \times 10^{-2}\alpha - 1.6 \times 10^{-2} = 0\)

The quadratic equation in \(\alpha\) can be solved and the two values of the roots are:

\(\alpha = +0.12\) and \(-0.12\)

The negative root is not acceptable and hence, \(\alpha = 0.12\)

This means that the degree of ionization, \(\alpha = 0.12\), then equilibrium concentrations of other species viz., \(\text{HF}\), \(\text{F}^-\) and \(\text{H}_3\text{O}^+\) are given by:

\([\text{H}_3\text{O}^+] = [\text{F}^-] = c\alpha = 0.02 \times 0.12 = 2.4 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{M}\)

\([\text{HF}] = c(1-\alpha) = 0.02(1-0.12) = 17.6 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{M}\)

\(\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+] = -\log(2.4 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.62\)
_note: The stem's K_a for HF (3.2e-4) differs from the value the chapter's own Table 6.6 prints for hydrofluoric acid (3.5e-4). The printed solution uses 3.2e-4 consistently throughout, so the worked example is internally coherent; the discrepancy is with the table only.

stem: The pH of \(0.1\,\text{M}\) monobasic acid is 4.50. Calculate the concentration of species \(\text{H}^+\), \(\text{A}^-\) and \(\text{HA}\) at equilibrium. Also, determine the value of \(K_a\) and \(\text{p}K_a\) of the monobasic acid.
solution:
\(\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+]\)

Therefore, \([\text{H}^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}} = 10^{-4.50} = 3.16 \times 10^{-5}\)

\([\text{H}^+] = [\text{A}^-] = 3.16 \times 10^{-5}\)

Thus, \(K_a = [\text{H}^+][\text{A}^-]/[\text{HA}]\)

\([\text{HA}]_{\text{eqlbm}} = 0.1 - (3.16 \times 10^{-5}) \simeq 0.1\)

\(K_a = (3.16 \times 10^{-5})^2/0.1 = 1.0 \times 10^{-8}\)

\(\text{p}K_a = -\log(10^{-8}) = 8\)

Alternatively, "Percent dissociation" is another useful method for measure of strength of a weak acid and is given as:

Percent dissociation \(= [\text{HA}]_{\text{dissociated}}/[\text{HA}]_{\text{initial}} \times 100\%\)

stem: Calculate the pH of \(0.08\,\text{M}\) solution of hypochlorous acid, \(\text{HOCl}\). The ionization constant of the acid is \(2.5 \times 10^{-5}\). Determine the percent dissociation of \(\text{HOCl}\).
solution:
\(\text{HOCl}(aq) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightleftharpoons \text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq) + \text{ClO}^-(aq)\)

Initial concentration (M): \(0.08\), \(0\), \(0\)

Change to reach equilibrium concentration (M): \(-x\), \(+x\), \(+x\)

Equilibrium concentration (M): \(0.08 - x\), \(x\), \(x\)

\(K_a = \{[\text{H}_3\text{O}^+][\text{ClO}^-]/[\text{HOCl}]\} = x^2/(0.08 - x)\)

As \(x \ll 0.08\), therefore \(0.08 - x \simeq 0.08\)

\(x^2/0.08 = 2.5 \times 10^{-5}\)

\(x^2 = 2.0 \times 10^{-6}\), thus, \(x = 1.41 \times 10^{-3}\)

\([\text{H}^+] = 1.41 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{M}\).

Therefore,

Percent dissociation \(= \{[\text{HOCl}]_{\text{dissociated}}/[\text{HOCl}]_{\text{initial}}\} \times 100 = 1.41 \times 10^{-3} \times 10^2/0.08 = 1.76\%\).

\(\text{pH} = -\log(1.41 \times 10^{-3}) = 2.85\).

stem: The pH of \(0.004\,\text{M}\) hydrazine solution is 9.7. Calculate its ionization constant \(K_b\) and \(\text{p}K_b\).
solution:
\(\text{NH}_2\text{NH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_2\text{NH}_3^+ + \text{OH}^-\)

From the pH we can calculate the hydrogen ion concentration. Knowing hydrogen ion concentration and the ionic product of water we can calculate the concentration of hydroxyl ions. Thus we have:

\([\text{H}^+] = \text{antilog}(-\text{pH}) = \text{antilog}(-9.7) = 1.67 \times 10^{-10}\)

\([\text{OH}^-] = K_w/[\text{H}^+] = 1 \times 10^{-14}/1.67 \times 10^{-10} = 5.98 \times 10^{-5}\)

The concentration of the corresponding hydrazinium ion is also the same as that of hydroxyl ion. The concentration of both these ions is very small so the concentration of the undissociated base can be taken equal to \(0.004\,\text{M}\).

Thus,

\(K_b = [\text{NH}_2\text{NH}_3^+][\text{OH}^-]/[\text{NH}_2\text{NH}_2] = (5.98 \times 10^{-5})^2/0.004 = 8.96 \times 10^{-7}\)

\(\text{p}K_b = -\log K_b = -\log(8.96 \times 10^{-7}) = 6.04\).

stem: Calculate the pH of the solution in which \(0.2\,\text{M}\) \(\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}\) and \(0.1\,\text{M}\) \(\text{NH}_3\) are present. The \(\text{p}K_b\) of ammonia solution is 4.75.
solution:
\(\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^-\)

The ionization constant of \(\text{NH}_3\),

\(K_b = \text{antilog}(-\text{p}K_b)\) i.e.

\(K_b = 10^{-4.75} = 1.77 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{M}\)

\(\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^-\)

Initial concentration (M): \(0.10\), \(0.20\), \(0\)

Change to reach equilibrium (M): \(-x\), \(+x\), \(+x\)

At equilibrium (M): \(0.10 - x\), \(0.20 + x\), \(x\)

\(K_b = [\text{NH}_4^+][\text{OH}^-]/[\text{NH}_3] = (0.20 + x)(x)/(0.1 - x) = 1.77 \times 10^{-5}\)

As \(K_b\) is small, we can neglect \(x\) in comparison to \(0.1\,\text{M}\) and \(0.2\,\text{M}\). Thus,

\([\text{OH}^-] = x = 0.88 \times 10^{-5}\)

Therefore, \([\text{H}^+] = 1.12 \times 10^{-9}\)

\(\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+] = 8.95\).

stem: Determine the degree of ionization and pH of a \(0.05\,\text{M}\) of ammonia solution. The ionization constant of ammonia can be taken from Table 6.7. Also, calculate the ionization constant of the conjugate acid of ammonia.
solution:
The ionization of \(\text{NH}_3\) in water is represented by equation:

\(\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^-\)

We use equation (6.33) to calculate hydroxyl ion concentration,

\([\text{OH}^-] = c\alpha = 0.05\alpha\)

\(K_b = 0.05\alpha^2/(1-\alpha)\)

The value of \(\alpha\) is small, therefore the quadratic equation can be simplified by neglecting \(\alpha\) in comparison to 1 in the denominator on right hand side of the equation,

Thus,

\(K_b = c\alpha^2\) or \(\alpha = \sqrt{1.77 \times 10^{-5}/0.05} = 0.018\).

\([\text{OH}^-] = c\alpha = 0.05 \times 0.018 = 9.4 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{M}\).

\([\text{H}^+] = K_w/[\text{OH}^-] = 10^{-14}/(9.4 \times 10^{-4}) = 1.06 \times 10^{-11}\)

\(\text{pH} = -\log(1.06 \times 10^{-11}) = 10.97\).

Now, using the relation for conjugate acid-base pair,

\(K_a \times K_b = K_w\)

using the value of \(K_b\) of \(\text{NH}_3\) from Table 6.7.

We can determine the concentration of conjugate acid \(\text{NH}_4^+\)

\(K_a = K_w/K_b = 10^{-14}/1.77 \times 10^{-5} = 5.64 \times 10^{-10}\).

stem: Calculate the pH of a \(0.10\,\text{M}\) ammonia solution. Calculate the pH after \(50.0\,\text{mL}\) of this solution is treated with \(25.0\,\text{mL}\) of \(0.10\,\text{M}\) \(\text{HCl}\). The dissociation constant of ammonia, \(K_b = 1.77 \times 10^{-5}\)
solution:
\(\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^-\)

\(K_b = [\text{NH}_4^+][\text{OH}^-]/[\text{NH}_3] = 1.77 \times 10^{-5}\)

Before neutralization,

\([\text{NH}_4^+] = [\text{OH}^-] = x\)

\([\text{NH}_3] = 0.10 - x \simeq 0.10\)

\(x^2/0.10 = 1.77 \times 10^{-5}\)

Thus, \(x = 1.33 \times 10^{-3} = [\text{OH}^-]\)

Therefore, \([\text{H}^+] = K_w/[\text{OH}^-] = 10^{-14}/(1.33 \times 10^{-3}) = 7.51 \times 10^{-12}\)

\(\text{pH} = -\log(7.5 \times 10^{-12}) = 11.12\)

On addition of \(25\,\text{mL}\) of \(0.1\,\text{M}\) \(\text{HCl}\) solution (i.e., \(2.5\,\text{mmol}\) of \(\text{HCl}\)) to \(50\,\text{mL}\) of \(0.1\,\text{M}\) ammonia solution (i.e., \(5\,\text{mmol}\) of \(\text{NH}_3\)), \(2.5\,\text{mmol}\) of ammonia molecules are neutralized. The resulting \(75\,\text{mL}\) solution contains the remaining unneutralized \(2.5\,\text{mmol}\) of \(\text{NH}_3\) molecules and \(2.5\,\text{mmol}\) of \(\text{NH}_4^+\).

\(\text{NH}_3 + \text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{Cl}^-\)

Initially: \(2.5\), \(2.5\), \(0\), \(0\)

At equilibrium: \(0\), \(0\), \(2.5\), \(2.5\)

The resulting \(75\,\text{mL}\) of solution contains \(2.5\,\text{mmol}\) of \(\text{NH}_4^+\) ions (i.e., \(0.033\,\text{M}\)) and \(2.5\,\text{mmol}\) (i.e., \(0.033\,\text{M}\)) of uneutralised \(\text{NH}_3\) molecules. This \(\text{NH}_3\) exists in the following equilibrium:

\(\text{NH}_4\text{OH} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^-\)

\(0.033\,\text{M} - y\), \(y\), \(y\)

where, \(y = [\text{OH}^-] = [\text{NH}_4^+]\)

The final \(75\,\text{mL}\) solution after neutralisation already contains \(2.5\,\text{mmol}\) \(\text{NH}_4^+\) ions (i.e. \(0.033\,\text{M}\)), thus total concentration of \(\text{NH}_4^+\) ions is given as:

\([\text{NH}_4^+] = 0.033 + y\)

As \(y\) is small, \([\text{NH}_4\text{OH}] \simeq 0.033\,\text{M}\) and \([\text{NH}_4^+] \simeq 0.033\,\text{M}\).

We know,

\(K_b = [\text{NH}_4^+][\text{OH}^-]/[\text{NH}_4\text{OH}] = y(0.033)/(0.033) = 1.77 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{M}\)

Thus, \(y = 1.77 \times 10^{-5} = [\text{OH}^-]\)

\([\text{H}^+] = 10^{-14}/1.77 \times 10^{-5} = 0.56 \times 10^{-9}\)

Hence, \(\text{pH} = 9.24\)

stem: The values of \(K_{sp}\) of two sparingly soluble salts \(\text{Ni(OH)}_2\) and \(\text{AgCN}\) are \(2.0 \times 10^{-15}\) and \(6 \times 10^{-17}\) respectively. Which salt is more soluble? Explain.
solution:
\(\text{AgCN} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ag}^+ + \text{CN}^-\)

\(K_{sp} = [\text{Ag}^+][\text{CN}^-] = 6 \times 10^{-17}\)

\(\text{Ni(OH)}_2 \rightleftharpoons \text{Ni}^{2+} + 2\text{OH}^-\)

\(K_{sp} = [\text{Ni}^{2+}][\text{OH}^-]^2 = 2 \times 10^{-15}\)

Let \([\text{Ag}^+] = S_1\), then \([\text{CN}^-] = S_1\)

Let \([\text{Ni}^{2+}] = S_2\), then \([\text{OH}^-] = 2S_2\)

\(S_1^2 = 6 \times 10^{-17}\), \(S_1 = 7.8 \times 10^{-9}\)

\((S_2)(2S_2)^2 = 2 \times 10^{-15}\), \(S_2 = 0.58 \times 10^{-4}\)

\(\text{Ni(OH)}_2\) is more soluble than \(\text{AgCN}\).

subtopic: Solubility Equilibria of Sparingly Soluble Salts
stem: Calculate the molar solubility of \(\text{Ni(OH)}_2\) in \(0.10\,\text{M}\) \(\text{NaOH}\). The ionic product of \(\text{Ni(OH)}_2\) is \(2.0 \times 10^{-15}\).
solution:
Let the solubility of \(\text{Ni(OH)}_2\) be equal to \(S\).

Dissolution of \(S\,\text{mol/L}\) of \(\text{Ni(OH)}_2\) provides \(S\,\text{mol/L}\) of \(\text{Ni}^{2+}\) and \(2S\,\text{mol/L}\) of \(\text{OH}^-\), but the total concentration of \(\text{OH}^- = (0.10 + 2S)\,\text{mol/L}\) because the solution already contains \(0.10\,\text{mol/L}\) of \(\text{OH}^-\) from \(\text{NaOH}\).

\(K_{sp} = 2.0 \times 10^{-15} = [\text{Ni}^{2+}][\text{OH}^-]^2 = (S)(0.10 + 2S)^2\)

As \(K_{sp}\) is small, \(2S \ll 0.10\), thus, \((0.10 + 2S) \approx 0.10\)

Hence,

\(2.0 \times 10^{-15} = S(0.10)^2\)

\(S = 2.0 \times 10^{-13}\,\text{M} = [\text{Ni}^{2+}]\)

If the second dissociation constant of \(\text{H}_2\text{S}\) is \(1.2 \times 10^{-13}\), calculate the concentration of \(\text{S}^{2-}\) under both conditions.

The ionization constant of acetic acid is \(1.74 \times 10^{-5}\). Calculate the degree of dissociation of acetic acid in its \(0.05\,\text{M}\) solution. Calculate the concentration of acetate ion in the solution and its pH.
It has been found that the pH of a \(0.01\,\text{M}\) solution of an organic acid is 4.15. Calculate the concentration of the anion, the ionization constant of the acid and its \(\text{p}K_a\).

Assuming complete dissociation, calculate the pH of the following solutions:

(a) \(0.003\,\text{M}\) \(\text{HCl}\) (b) \(0.005\,\text{M}\) \(\text{NaOH}\) (c) \(0.002\,\text{M}\) \(\text{HBr}\) (d) \(0.002\,\text{M}\) \(\text{KOH}\)

Calculate the pH of the following solutions:

a) \(2\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{TlOH}\) dissolved in water to give \(2\) litre of solution.

b) \(0.3\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{Ca(OH)}_2\) dissolved in water to give \(500\,\text{mL}\) of solution.

c) \(0.3\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{NaOH}\) dissolved in water to give \(200\,\text{mL}\) of solution.

d) \(1\,\text{mL}\) of \(13.6\,\text{M}\) \(\text{HCl}\) is diluted with water to give \(1\) litre of solution.
The degree of ionization of a \(0.1\,\text{M}\) bromoacetic acid solution is 0.132. Calculate the pH of the solution and the \(\text{p}K_a\) of bromoacetic acid.
The pH of \(0.005\,\text{M}\) codeine \((\text{C}_{18}\text{H}_{21}\text{NO}_3)\) solution is 9.95. Calculate its ionization constant and \(\text{p}K_b\).

What is the pH of \(0.001\,\text{M}\) aniline solution? The ionization constant of aniline can be taken from Table 6.7. Calculate the degree of ionization of aniline in the solution. Also calculate the ionization constant of the conjugate acid of aniline.

Calculate the degree of ionization of \(0.05\,\text{M}\) acetic acid if its \(\text{p}K_a\) value is 4.74. How is the degree of dissociation affected when its solution also contains (a) \(0.01\,\text{M}\) (b) \(0.1\,\text{M}\) in \(\text{HCl}\)?

The ionization constant of dimethylamine is \(5.4 \times 10^{-4}\). Calculate its degree of ionization in its \(0.02\,\text{M}\) solution. What percentage of dimethylamine is ionized if the solution is also \(0.1\,\text{M}\) in \(\text{NaOH}\)?

Calculate the hydrogen ion concentration in the following biological fluids whose pH are given below:

(a) Human muscle-fluid, 6.83

(b) Human stomach fluid, 1.2

(c) Human blood, 7.38

(d) Human saliva, 6.4.
The pH of milk, black coffee, tomato juice, lemon juice and egg white are 6.8, 5.0, 4.2, 2.2 and 7.8 respectively. Calculate corresponding hydrogen ion concentration in each.
If \(0.561\,\text{g}\) of \(\text{KOH}\) is dissolved in water to give \(200\,\text{mL}\) of solution at 298 K. Calculate the concentrations of potassium, hydrogen and hydroxyl ions. What is its pH?
The solubility of \(\text{Sr(OH)}_2\) at 298 K is \(19.23\,\text{g/L}\) of solution. Calculate the concentrations of strontium and hydroxyl ions and the pH of the solution.

The ionization constant of propanoic acid is \(1.32 \times 10^{-5}\). Calculate the degree of ionization of the acid in its \(0.05\,\text{M}\) solution and also its pH. What will be its degree of ionization if the solution is \(0.01\,\text{M}\) in \(\text{HCl}\) also?
The pH of \(0.1\,\text{M}\) solution of cyanic acid \((\text{HCNO})\) is 2.34. Calculate the ionization constant of the acid and its degree of ionization in the solution.
The ionization constant of nitrous acid is \(4.5 \times 10^{-4}\). Calculate the pH of \(0.04\,\text{M}\) sodium nitrite solution and also its degree of hydrolysis.
A \(0.02\,\text{M}\) solution of pyridinium hydrochloride has \(\text{pH} = 3.44\). Calculate the ionization constant of pyridine.

Predict if the solutions of the following salts are neutral, acidic or basic:

\(\text{NaCl}\), \(\text{KBr}\), \(\text{NaCN}\), \(\text{NH}_4\text{NO}_3\), \(\text{NaNO}_2\) and \(\text{KF}\)
The ionization constant of chloroacetic acid is \(1.35 \times 10^{-3}\). What will be the pH of \(0.1\,\text{M}\) acid and its \(0.1\,\text{M}\) sodium salt solution?
Ionic product of water at 310 K is \(2.7 \times 10^{-14}\). What is the pH of neutral water at this temperature?

Calculate the pH of the resultant mixtures:

a) \(10\,\text{mL}\) of \(0.2\,\text{M}\) \(\text{Ca(OH)}_2 + 25\,\text{mL}\) of \(0.1\,\text{M}\) \(\text{HCl}\)

b) \(10\,\text{mL}\) of \(0.01\,\text{M}\) \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 + 10\,\text{mL}\) of \(0.01\,\text{M}\) \(\text{Ca(OH)}_2\)

c) \(10\,\text{mL}\) of \(0.1\,\text{M}\) \(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 + 10\,\text{mL}\) of \(0.1\,\text{M}\) \(\text{KOH}\)

subtopic: Solubility Equilibria of Sparingly Soluble Salts
stem: Equal volumes of \(0.002\,\text{M}\) solutions of sodium iodate and cupric chlorate are mixed together. Will it lead to precipitation of copper iodate? (For cupric iodate \(K_{sp} = 7.4 \times 10^{-8}\)).

subtopic: Solubility Equilibria of Sparingly Soluble Salts
stem: The ionization constant of benzoic acid is \(6.46 \times 10^{-5}\) and \(K_{sp}\) for silver benzoate is \(2.5 \times 10^{-13}\). How many times is silver benzoate more soluble in a buffer of \(\text{pH } 3.19\) compared to its solubility in pure water?

subtopic: Solubility Equilibria of Sparingly Soluble Salts
stem: What is the maximum concentration of equimolar solutions of ferrous sulphate and sodium sulphide so that when mixed in equal volumes, there is no precipitation of iron sulphide? (For iron sulphide, \(K_{sp} = 6.3 \times 10^{-18}\)).

subtopic: Solubility Equilibria of Sparingly Soluble Salts
stem: What is the minimum volume of water required to dissolve \(1\,\text{g}\) of calcium sulphate at 298 K? (For calcium sulphate, \(K_{sp}\) is \(9.1 \times 10^{-6}\)).

subtopic: Solubility Equilibria of Sparingly Soluble Salts

If \(10\,\text{mL}\) of this is added to \(5\,\text{mL}\) of \(0.04\,\text{M}\) solution of the following: \(\text{FeSO}_4\), \(\text{MnCl}_2\), \(\text{ZnCl}_2\) and \(\text{CdCl}_2\), in which of these solutions precipitation will take place?
